sun.declination_note: Northern-summer solstice: the Sun reaches the table's sun_elev_max_deg (69.04 deg = 90 - 22.5 + 1.54) at local noon, in the south. Illustrative choice of season; other seasons change the noon Sun by at most 3.1 deg.
sun.window_note: One lunar daytime, from shortly after sunrise (Sun 1.5 deg up) to shortly before sunset: 178 deg of the 181.3 deg of hour angle between flat-horizon sunrise and sunset (14.6 of the 14.9 Earth days of daylight). The other half of the 29.53-day cycle is night (shaded on the graph).

earth_visibility.decision: Not drawn. At its mean position (the sub-Earth point at 0 N 0 E; elevation 90 deg minus the 22.8 deg arc from the site, az 170.9 deg; parallax and libration ignored, a geometric estimate) the Earth stands about 67 deg up in the south, above the camera's field of view for most of the video.

array.assumption: Illustrative engineering shape, not a real design: short mast, hub 2.4 m above ground; two wings of 3 hinged panels, each panel 2.0 m x 1.2 m (total 14.4 m2), that unfold upwards and end flat (horizontal, tilt 0 deg), as the mission's irradiance (a horizontal surface) assumes. No tracking.

panel_text.model_tag: Model: S0 1361 W/m² × sin(Sun elev.) × visible disc, flat panel, before cell efficiency. Lunar day: 29.5 Earth days, about half of it night.

render.lighting_note: Sun: one parallel light of fixed intensity (3.2 in renderer units, chosen so that the high noon Sun does not saturate the light-grey ground); terrain shadows from the real SLDEM2015 horizons; 3.5 % uniform fill (assumption). Display exposure (a camera setting; the light and the power are not changed): min(8, max(1, sin 25° / sin h)), h = Sun elevation; stated on screen whenever it is above 1.25.

card.title: Earth analog and lunar twin: solar panels, pair number 1
card.subtitle: Suitability 96.9, similarity 99.99, final 98.45. The lunar cell lies in the low equatorial plains (the maria), the Solar panels zone: within 30° of the equator and at or below −1,200 m. Values from the project tables (1-degree cells); each carries its level.

rows.label: Sunlight above the atmosphere
rows.earth_note: top of the atmosphere, formula from latitude

card.legend: Sunlight above the atmosphere: on Earth, the annual-mean daily sunlight on a horizontal surface at the top of the atmosphere, from the cell's latitude (a formula); on the Moon, the table's surface irradiance (horizontal, S0 = 1361 W/m², averaged over the whole lunar cycle, nights included). Sunlight reaching the ground on Earth: WorldClim 2.1, modelled (non-commercial licence). A panel at the Earth site receives only the sunlight that reaches the ground. The Solar panels similarity is saturated. Sunlight above the atmosphere depends on latitude only, so almost every Earth point finds many cells of the equatorial maria that match it almost exactly: its twin is the best of a median of about 1,840 candidate cells that pass the tolerances, 78 % of the 6,360 pairs score 99 or more and 514 show 100.00. Here a high similarity says that the pair is within the tolerances, not that it is closer than another pair: read the real differences shown beside it (sunlight above the atmosphere, slope and roughness). Among the 100 best-ranked points the similarity only goes from 99.88 to 100.00, so their order follows suitability.

pair_values.source: app/public/data/v2/explain.json, missions.solar item with rank 1; similarity.json (display rule of the share lost, saturation note, lunar day); missions.json and mission_zones.json (zone); variables.json and missions.json similarity sides (levels). prepare.py checks every value here against those files, and render.js runs that check before it renders.
pair_values.pair_sentence: This pair is matched on sunlight above the atmosphere: 9.6 kWh/m²/day at the top of Earth's atmosphere here and 9.6 kWh/m²/day on the lunar surface. At the Earth site only 6.2 of those 9.6 kWh/m²/day reach the ground (35 % is lost in the atmosphere), while the Moon has no atmosphere and its day lasts 29.5 Earth days, about half of them in darkness. Terrain (slope and roughness) is a secondary criterion.

en.header: Solar panels mission video (3D simulation), English descriptive captions
en.note: No speech. Each cue gives the values on the on-screen panel at its start time; the panel status does not change within a cue. The Sun is computed; power and energy are a stated model for a flat (horizontal) panel per m², before any cell efficiency; array size and timing are illustrative. While the Sun is low the display exposure is raised (not to scale).

text: 3D simulation driven by table data, not real footage. Sunrise over the real relief (SLDEM2015, LOLA and Kaguya) of lunar cell M24296, 22.5° N 3.5° W, 75.8 km from the crater Huxley, in the low equatorial plains (the maria). The Sun is just above the eastern horizon; the exposure is raised for the low Sun (not to scale). The camera descends to the stowed panels.
The Sun climbs above 10°; the shadows shorten.
The mast rises and two wings of hinged panels unfold upwards.
The panels lie flat, facing the sky; energy is counted from now.
Morning: the Sun climbs in the east. The power of a flat panel follows the Sun's elevation (model, before cell efficiency).
The Sun is above 60°: short shadows and the most power.
Local noon: the Sun stands in the south at the cell's highest elevation in the table (69.04°).
Afternoon: the Sun descends towards the west; the shadows lengthen.
The power falls as the Sun gets lower. The lunar day lasts 29.5 Earth days and about half of it is night: after sunset a panel here gets no sunlight for about two Earth weeks (shaded on the graph).
Low Sun in the west: long shadows; the exposure is raised again (not to scale). Sunset and the lunar night follow.

Closing card: the Earth analog in Australia (cell E38464, 16.5° S 124.5° E, 128.7 km from Derby) and its lunar twin, cell M24296 near Huxley, matched on sunlight above the atmosphere: 9.6005 against 9.604 kWh/m² per day (difference 0.0035, tolerance 0.6). At the Earth site only 6.177 kWh/m² per day reach the ground (modelled): 6.2 of 9.6, 35 % is lost in the atmosphere; the Moon has no atmosphere. Slope 0.976° against 1.047°; roughness 39.2 m against 39.03 m. Suitability 96.9, similarity 99.99, final 98.45.

A panel at the Earth site does not receive what a panel on the Moon receives: only the sunlight that reaches the ground arrives there, while the Moon's day lasts 29.5 Earth days, about half of them dark. Mean surface temperature 302.37 K against 213.39 K and daily swing 11.89 K against 293.36 K are not part of the similarity. 3D simulation driven by table data. Not real footage.

es.header: Vídeo de la misión de paneles solares (simulación 3D), subtítulos descriptivos en español
es.note: Sin voz. Cada subtítulo da los valores del panel en pantalla al inicio del subtítulo; el estado del panel no cambia dentro de un subtítulo. El Sol es calculado; potencia y energía son un modelo declarado para un panel plano (horizontal) por m², antes de la eficiencia de las células; el tamaño de los paneles y los tiempos son ilustrativos. Mientras el Sol está bajo se aumenta la exposición de la imagen (no a escala).

text: Simulación 3D basada en datos de las tablas, no son imágenes reales. Amanecer sobre el relieve real (SLDEM2015, LOLA y Kaguya) de la celda lunar M24296, 22,5° N 3,5° O, a 75,8 km del cráter Huxley, en las llanuras ecuatoriales bajas (los mares). El Sol acaba de asomar por el horizonte este; la exposición se aumenta por el Sol bajo (no a escala). La cámara desciende hasta los paneles plegados.
El Sol pasa de 10°; las sombras se acortan.
El mástil sube y dos alas de paneles con bisagras se despliegan hacia arriba.
Los paneles quedan en horizontal, mirando al cielo; la energía se cuenta desde ahora.
Mañana: el Sol sube por el este. La potencia de un panel plano sigue la altura del Sol (modelo, antes de la eficiencia de las células).
El Sol pasa de 60°: sombras cortas y la máxima potencia.
Mediodía local: el Sol está al sur, a la altura máxima de la celda según la tabla (69,04°).
Tarde: el Sol baja hacia el oeste; las sombras se alargan.

La potencia cae a medida que el Sol baja. El día lunar dura 29,5 días terrestres y aproximadamente la mitad es de noche: tras la puesta de Sol un panel aquí no recibe luz durante unas dos semanas terrestres (sombreado en la gráfica).
Sol bajo al oeste: sombras largas; la exposición vuelve a aumentarse (no a escala). Después llegan la puesta de Sol y la noche lunar.

Tarjeta final: el análogo terrestre en Australia (celda E38464, 16,5° S 124,5° E, a 128,7 km de Derby) y su gemela lunar, la celda M24296 cerca de Huxley, emparejadas por la luz solar por encima de la atmósfera: 9,6005 frente a 9,604 kWh/m² al día (diferencia 0,0035, tolerancia 0,6). En el punto terrestre solo 6,177 kWh/m² al día llegan al suelo (modelado): 6,2 de 9,6, se pierde un 35 % en la atmósfera; la Luna no tiene atmósfera. Pendiente 0,976° frente a 1,047°; rugosidad 39,2 m frente a 39,03 m. Idoneidad 96,9, similitud 99,99, final 98,45.

Un panel en el punto terrestre no recibe lo mismo que un panel en la Luna: allí solo llega la luz que alcanza el suelo, mientras que el día lunar dura 29,5 días terrestres, aproximadamente la mitad a oscuras. La temperatura media de la superficie, 302,37 K frente a 213,39 K, y la oscilación diaria, 11,89 K frente a 293,36 K, no forman parte de la similitud. Simulación 3D basada en datos de las tablas. No son imágenes reales.
